section_summary: This section combines public advocacy and constituent correspondence urging the United States to stop supplying Japan with scrap iron, petroleum, aircraft material, and other war-related commodities, with repeated State Department explanations that new legislation would be required for most embargoes. It also documents Philippine anti-Japanese organizations, reports of German military assistance to Japan, and inquiries from businesses about prospective export restrictions. The final portion concerns efforts by the State, War, and Navy Departments to discourage American oil companies from transferring high-octane aviation-gasoline technology to Japanese interests, including a detailed technical memorandum on production processes.

subfiles.title: Leaflet advocating American non-participation in Japanese aggression
subfiles.from: American Committee for Non-Participation in Japanese Aggression
subfiles.about: Advocates ending American exports that sustain Japan's war in China.
subfiles.summary: The leaflet argues that public opinion favors stopping war supplies to Japan and that treaty rights and obligations provide a legal and moral basis for action. It presents an embargo as a middle course between continued material support and direct military intervention, describes the committee's nationwide campaign, and solicits public participation and donations.

subfiles.title: Harry B. Price to Joseph C. Green requesting an appointment
subfiles.about: Requests a Washington meeting to discuss questions concerning the committee's campaign.
subfiles.summary: Price recalls an earlier meeting with Mr. Post during Green's absence. He says he will be in Washington the following day and asks to telephone Green's office to arrange a convenient appointment.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Harry B. Price's meeting with the Division of Controls
subfiles.about: Records Price's questions about trade restrictions, David Warren Ryder, and foreign-agent registration.
subfiles.summary: Price sought administrative advice about proposed restrictions on trade with Japan and asked whether David Warren Ryder was registered as an agent of a foreign principal. Green disclosed confidentially that the Justice Department was investigating Ryder and advised that occasional small Chinese donations would not require Price's organization to register.

subfiles.title: Under Secretary's routing note on the Hyslop correspondence
subfiles.from: Office of the Under Secretary of State
subfiles.to: Stanley K. Hornbeck and Mr. Hamilton
subfiles.about: Asks State Department officials to prepare an answer to an incoming letter.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary forwards a letter for handling by Hornbeck and Hamilton. The brief note appears to concern F. E. Hyslop's criticism of State Department export policy.

subfiles.title: F. E. Hyslop to Sumner Welles on exports to Japan
subfiles.about: Challenges the State Department to justify continued American exports useful to Japan's war effort.
subfiles.summary: Hyslop contrasts earlier assurances about munitions licenses with reports that the United States continued to supply much of Japan's war equipment. He asks how such exports can be reconciled with Hull's and Welles's professions of support for peace and encloses critical newspaper clippings.

subfiles.title: Newspaper clippings on arms exports and British cargo seizures
subfiles.to: Enclosed with F. E. Hyslop's letter
subfiles.about: Presents allegations about arms shipments to Germany and reports British seizures of contraband from American vessels.
subfiles.summary: One clipping asserts that Cordell Hull allowed arms shipments to Germany until the neutrality embargo took effect despite treaty objections raised by Senator Nye and others. A second reports British seizure of German-bound cargoes from American ships and their expected review by a prize court.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to F. E. Hyslop on export controls
subfiles.from: Joseph C. Green, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Explains the narrow statutory authority for restricting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Green states that only three arms-export licenses for Japan had been issued since December 1938 and refers Hyslop to an earlier explanation of the DC-4 sale. He adds that existing law did not permit bans on scrap iron, petroleum, machine tools, or similar goods, making new legislation necessary.

subfiles.title: Interior Department transmittal of the Philippine embargo petition
subfiles.about: Transmits a radiogram concerning a Philippine petition for an embargo on shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Interior Department sends the State Department a copy of High Commissioner Sayre's radiogram. The radiogram reports a petition demanding an embargo on munitions and other war commodities destined for Japan.

subfiles.title: Francis B. Sayre radiogram reporting the Philippine petition
subfiles.about: Reports a petition said to bear more than 48,000 Philippine signatures urging an immediate embargo against Japan.
subfiles.summary: Sayre quotes the petition's demand that the United States prevent shipments of munitions and war commodities to Japanese aggressors. He identifies the sponsoring organizations and states that he is forwarding the petition for transmission to Congress and other appropriate offices.

subfiles.title: Office of Philippine Affairs memorandum on handling the petition
subfiles.about: Recommends leaving transmission of the Philippine petition to Congress to the Interior Department.
subfiles.summary: Jacobs concludes that the State Department need take no action because the petition was sent through the Department of the Interior. He recommends informing Interior that State assumes the Secretary of the Interior will decide whether to transmit it to Congress.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Harold L. Ickes on the Philippine petition
subfiles.from: Henry F. Grady, for the Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Leaves disposition of the Philippine embargo petition to the Interior Department.
subfiles.summary: The letter acknowledges the petition of more than 48,000 Philippine residents seeking an embargo on war shipments to Japan. Because it was transmitted to Interior, Grady states that Ickes may take whatever action he considers appropriate regarding its submission to Congress.

subfiles.title: Carl H. Mote to Cordell Hull requesting information
subfiles.about: Requests information about the State Department's policy on aeronautical exports to countries bombing civilians.
subfiles.summary: Although much of the OCR is illegible, the subsequent reply identifies Mote's request as concerning Hull's statement on aeronautical supplies. The letter prompted the Department to send the National Munitions Control Board's annual report and its July 1938 circular to exporters.

subfiles.title: Promotional reviews of The New Deal Goose Step
subfiles.about: Collects reviews and testimonials promoting Carl H. Mote's book The New Deal Goose Step.
subfiles.summary: The sheet quotes reviewers who praise Mote's attack on the New Deal, communism, and President Roosevelt. Personal testimonials emphasize the book's readability and provocative character.

subfiles.title: Charles W. Yost to Carl H. Mote on aeronautical export policy
subfiles.about: Provides official material concerning restrictions on aeronautical exports and licenses issued for Japan.
subfiles.summary: Yost encloses the National Munitions Control Board's third annual report, including the Department's July 1, 1938 letter to aircraft manufacturers and exporters. He states that only three licenses covering arms, ammunition, implements of war, or aircraft had been issued for Japan since December 1938.

subfiles.title: Edwin C. Barringer telegram on a rumored scrap-iron embargo
subfiles.about: Requests immediate clarification of a report that an embargo on scrap shipments to Japan would begin on January 26.
subfiles.summary: Barringer cites a Seattle speech attributed to Representative Magnuson and warns that the report is disturbing Pacific Coast trade and may affect contracts. He asks whether, as he understands, specific legislation would be required before the executive branch could impose such an embargo.

subfiles.title: State Department telegram to Edwin C. Barringer
subfiles.about: Confirms that the executive branch lacked authority to embargo scrap-iron shipments to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department tells Barringer that his understanding is correct. Specific legislation would be necessary to impose an embargo on iron and steel scrap exports to Japan.

subfiles.title: Martin F. Smith transmittal of the Port of Vancouver inquiry
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's request for information about a possible embargo affecting the Port of Vancouver.
subfiles.summary: Smith encloses a letter from T. P. MacComber, manager of the Port of Vancouver. He asks Hull for an expression of the Department's position that can be transmitted to his constituent.

subfiles.title: T. P. MacComber to Martin F. Smith on scrap-iron shipments
subfiles.about: Asks whether a scrap-iron embargo is likely after termination of the 1911 commercial treaty with Japan.
subfiles.summary: MacComber explains that export brokers are considering using Port of Vancouver facilities for shipments of scrap iron to Japan. Before committing the port, he seeks clarification of an Associated Press report attributing an imminent embargo to Representative Magnuson.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Martin F. Smith on scrap-iron controls
subfiles.about: Explains that new legislation would be required to prohibit scrap-iron exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull states that no existing law authorizes a prohibition on scrap-iron exports to any foreign country. Several bills addressing war materials had been introduced, but Congress had not acted on them.

subfiles.title: Lyndon B. Johnson transmittal of Caroline Crowell's letter
subfiles.about: Forwards a constituent's proposal for changing American policy toward Japan.
subfiles.summary: Johnson encloses a letter from Dr. Caroline Crowell of the University of Texas Health Service. He asks the Secretary of State to give her foreign-policy views thoughtful attention.

subfiles.title: Caroline Crowell to Lyndon B. Johnson advocating economic pressure on Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an end to supplies for Japan and, if necessary, a boycott of Japanese silk.
subfiles.summary: Crowell argues that Japan depends on the United States for the supplies needed to continue its war in China. She believes an embargo and silk boycott could end the conflict, remove the Japanese threat in the Pacific, and allow Britain and France to concentrate on Germany.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Lyndon B. Johnson
subfiles.about: Explains why the government could not impose the embargo proposed by Caroline Crowell without new legislation.
subfiles.summary: The Department states that the Neutrality Act of 1939 did not authorize prohibition of arms exports to belligerents. Except for tin-plate scrap and helium, existing law likewise did not authorize bans on other manufactured goods or raw materials, and Congress had not acted on proposed Japan embargo bills.

subfiles.title: Interior Department transmittal on Philippine anti-Japanese organizations
subfiles.about: Forwards a High Commissioner's Office report on the organizations supporting the Philippine embargo petition.
subfiles.summary: The letter supplements Interior's earlier transmission of Sayre's radiogram. It encloses information about the purposes, leadership, and activities of several Filipino organizations associated with the petition.

subfiles.title: Woodbury Willoughby's report on Philippine organizations
subfiles.from: Woodbury Willoughby, Office of the High Commissioner
subfiles.to: Director, Division of Territories and Island Possessions
subfiles.about: Describes five Philippine organizations involved in anti-Japanese advocacy and the embargo petition.
subfiles.summary: Willoughby outlines the Friends of China, Chinese YMCA, League for the Defense of Democracy, Young Philippines, and Congress for Democracy and Collective Security. He discusses their educational, boycott, political, and relief activities, internal divisions, and conflicts with postal, police, and presidential authorities. He concludes that two of the more radical organizations had little influence and few members.

subfiles.title: Curtis W. Barnes memorandum on Leon Pearson's telephone inquiry
subfiles.about: Records a reporter's inquiry about West Coast stories predicting an immediate scrap-iron embargo.
subfiles.summary: Barnes directed Leon Pearson to the Far Eastern Division and Office of the Economic Adviser because scrap iron lay outside the Division of Controls' jurisdiction. He said the Department did not know the reports' inspiration and expressed a personal suspicion that a lobbyist was responsible, while confirming that no law then authorized such an embargo.

subfiles.title: Vic Donahey transmittal of four Mansfield constituent letters
subfiles.about: Forwards four constituent questions about the Sino-Japanese conflict for State Department answers.
subfiles.summary: Donahey sends letters from Mansfield, Ohio, concerning American neutrality, war-material exports, the Open Door, and the commercial treaty with Japan. He asks the Department to provide information that will satisfy the writers' questions.

subfiles.title: Fred Morey to Vic Donahey on American policy toward China and Japan
subfiles.about: Asks why the United States has not recognized a state of war and what effect stopping supplies to Japan would have.
subfiles.summary: Morey poses questions about the undeclared war, American munitions business, Japan's dependence on U.S. supplies, Chinese guerrilla prospects, and the Open Door. He also asks how the cash-and-carry system's apparent advantage to Japan might be remedied.

subfiles.title: Edward A. Eisele Jr. to Vic Donahey on the undeclared war
subfiles.about: Asks why the president has not declared that a state of war exists between China and Japan.
subfiles.summary: Eisele explains that a former newspaper correspondent's school talk prompted student discussion of the Sino-Japanese conflict. He says the scale of fighting appears plainly to constitute war and requests an explanation of the government's position.

subfiles.title: Dick Coleman to Vic Donahey on war-material sales and the Open Door
subfiles.about: Questions why the United States supplies Japan and how a Japanese victory would affect the Open Door policy.
subfiles.summary: Coleman notes widespread American sympathy for China and asks why the United States nevertheless sells war materials to Japan. He also requests Donahey's opinion on the consequences of a Japanese victory for American commercial access to China.

subfiles.title: Margie J. White to Vic Donahey on the 1911 treaty
subfiles.about: Requests information about the contents, benefits, expiration, and possible renewal of the commercial treaty with Japan.
subfiles.summary: White says she has heard conflicting reports about the war and the treaty with Japan. She wants factual information before forming or voicing her own opinion.

subfiles.title: Cordell Hull to Vic Donahey answering Mansfield constituents
subfiles.about: Answers questions about nonrecognition of a state of war, export controls, and the terminated commercial treaty with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Hull says the president concluded that formally finding a state of war would not serve the broad interests of the United States and its nationals. He explains the lack of statutory authority for most export prohibitions and notes that the United States gave notice on July 26, 1939, terminating the 1911 treaty. Any replacement treaty, he adds, would depend on future developments.

subfiles.title: Senate referral slip for Ben F. Mehr's letter
subfiles.about: Refers a constituent communication for consideration, report, and return.
subfiles.summary: The Senate form asks the Department to give the enclosed communication favorable consideration and prepare a report. The enclosure was Ben F. Mehr's letter about Japan, the Nine-Power Treaty, and embargo policy.

subfiles.title: Ben F. Mehr to Elmer Thomas on the Nine-Power Treaty and Japan
subfiles.about: Urges an embargo against Japan and asks why treaty rights and the Open Door are not being defended.
subfiles.summary: Mehr condemns exports of scrap iron, cotton, and other raw materials that aid Japan while threatening American markets in China. Drawing on his First World War service, he rejects another war but advocates an embargo strong enough to compel Japan to honor its commitments.

subfiles.title: State Department reply to Elmer Thomas on Ben F. Mehr's letter
subfiles.about: Provides a standard explanation of the legal limits on prohibiting exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The Department thanks Thomas for forwarding Mehr's letter and supplies language commonly used in responses of this kind. It explains that neither the Neutrality Act nor other existing laws, apart from provisions on tin-plate scrap and helium, authorized bans on arms, scrap iron, cotton, or similar exports without new legislation.

subfiles.title: Cross-reference note on altimeters for Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Controls, Joseph C. Green
subfiles.about: Points to a memorandum concerning an inquiry about exporting Western Electric altimeters to Japan.
subfiles.summary: The sheet records a telephone inquiry from Frank Page, an export agent, about the Department's attitude toward altimeter exports to Japan. It directs readers to the original memorandum filed under military secrets and armament-control records.

subfiles.title: Navy Department routing slip for an attaché report
subfiles.from: Office of the Chief of Naval Operations
subfiles.about: Routes an attached report concerning Japanese affairs for information and return.
subfiles.summary: The printed form lists Navy Department offices and circulation instructions. Handwritten annotations indicate that the attached intelligence report concerned Japanese matters and was to be returned after review.

subfiles.title: Naval attaché report on German military aid to Japan
subfiles.about: Reports claims that Germany sent technicians, aviators, munitions, and aircraft to Japan.
subfiles.summary: A source described as probably proven claimed that more than 450 former Condor Legion personnel were dispatched to Japan after returning from Spain, accompanied by two ships carrying munitions and aircraft from Amsterdam. The source attributed the assistance to the Japanese ambassador's efforts to promote a full German-Japanese military alliance.

subfiles.title: Arthur Nichols Young to Stanley K. Hornbeck requesting export statistics
subfiles.about: Requests figures for American exports of arms and strategically important commodities to Japan in 1938 and 1939.
subfiles.summary: Young asks for the values of arms and ammunition exported to Japan. He also requests figures and principal categories for other goods of military importance, such as gasoline.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck to Arthur Nichols Young with a Chinese economic study
subfiles.about: Sends a study comparing U.S. sales of war materials to Japan in 1937-1939.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck encloses a Chinese Council for Economic Research study covering the first eight months of 1939 and corresponding periods in 1938 and 1937. Although he cannot guarantee its statistics, he describes its compiler as an able Harvard-trained Chinese economist connected with the Brookings Institution and believes the report will meet Young's needs.

subfiles.title: Memorandum of Aluminum Company inquiries about exports to Japan
subfiles.to: Division of Controls and interested State Department offices
subfiles.about: Records questions about aluminum-ore exports, credit, and post-treaty trade with Japan.
subfiles.summary: Edward B. Wilber and Arthur P. Hall asked whether the aircraft moral embargo extended to aluminum ores and whether Neutrality Act credit restrictions applied to Japan. Allen replied that Japan had not been designated a belligerent, that ordinary laws such as the Johnson Act governed credit, and that the Department could not encourage credit to Japanese interests. He added that after the commercial treaty ended, trade would be governed by domestic and international law.

subfiles.title: Stanley K. Hornbeck note to Henry F. Grady on an outgoing letter
subfiles.about: Suggests that a sensitive outgoing reply be dated from Grady's residence rather than the State Department.
subfiles.summary: Hornbeck characterizes the suggestion as personal or semi-official. The adjacent assistant-secretary sheet appears to have accompanied preparation or routing of Grady's response to Carl Oppenheimer.

subfiles.title: Carl Oppenheimer to Mrs. Grady on an anti-oil-export campaign
subfiles.about: Asks whether a California campaign to stop oil exports to Japan would interfere with State Department plans.
subfiles.summary: Oppenheimer says his organization is considering launching a California campaign against oil shipments to Japan. Before proceeding, he asks whether the movement would conflict with State Department policy or plans.

subfiles.title: Henry F. Grady to Carl Oppenheimer on private anti-export activity
subfiles.about: Responds cautiously to Oppenheimer's proposed campaign against oil exports to Japan.
subfiles.summary: Grady says private conduct must remain a matter of individual judgment and conviction. He notes that Congress, not the executive branch, held the power to impose export embargoes and that several embargo bills introduced during the preceding session had not been enacted.

subfiles.title: Assistant Secretary's note returning the assembled aviation-gasoline file
subfiles.from: Office of the Assistant Secretary of State
subfiles.about: Thanks Green for assembling a historical file and reports that Adolf A. Berle Jr. has finished using it.
subfiles.summary: The note acknowledges Green's work collecting the file. It states that Berle appreciated the effort and had completed his review of the papers.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green to Adolf A. Berle Jr. transmitting an incomplete historical file
subfiles.about: Transmits papers on attempts to prevent Japan and the Soviet Union from receiving aviation-gasoline production technology.
subfiles.summary: Green sends the documents he had obtained from Departmental records following a telephone request. He notes that the file remains incomplete and promises to forward additional material if it can be located.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green supplementary transmittal of aviation-gasoline papers
subfiles.about: Forwards additional records on preventing disclosure of high-octane gasoline manufacturing information.
subfiles.summary: Green supplies further documents concerning plans, specifications, and production information sought by Japan and the Soviet Union. He again indicates that more records may be available from Departmental files.

subfiles.title: Joseph C. Green memorandum on proposed sales of aviation-gasoline technology to Japan
subfiles.to: State Department files and senior officials
subfiles.about: Records interdepartmental and industry discussions aimed at preventing the transfer of advanced aviation-gasoline processes to Japanese interests.
subfiles.summary: After approaches from the War Department and Frank Howard, Hornbeck, Welles, Admiral Stark, and Green agreed that the government should discourage sales of advanced aviation-gasoline technology to Japan. At a November 20 industry meeting, Howard advocated a blanket agreement, while E. B. Badger argued that his company was already morally committed to a Houdry-process project that would not materially increase Japanese capabilities. Because the competing firms could not agree, Badger proposed submitting his project for formal War and Navy Department review and promised to withdraw if the government found it contrary to policy.

subfiles.title: Telegram inviting Shell Oil to the December 14 conference
subfiles.to: R. R. Griffin, Shell Oil Company
subfiles.about: Invites a Shell Oil representative to a State Department meeting on aviation-gasoline technology.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary requests attendance at a December 14 meeting in Room 360 of the State Department Building. The telegram notes that other interested companies were receiving similar invitations.

subfiles.title: Telegram inviting Standard Oil and related companies to the December 14 conference
subfiles.to: Frank A. Howard and other interested oil companies
subfiles.about: Calls representatives of Standard Oil Development, E. B. Badger and Sons, Sun Oil, and Socony-Vacuum to a follow-up meeting.
subfiles.summary: The telegram asks Howard to send a representative to discuss further the matter raised in Green's office on November 20. Identical messages were designated for E. B. Badger and Sons, Sun Oil, and Socony-Vacuum.

subfiles.title: Telegram inviting Universal Oil Products and M. W. Kellogg
subfiles.to: Universal Oil Products Company and M. W. Kellogg Company
subfiles.about: Invites two process-technology companies to the December 14 State Department meeting.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary requests representatives for a discussion of a question affecting both the government and certain oil companies. The same text was to be sent to the M. W. Kellogg Company.

subfiles.title: Telegram inviting Phillips Petroleum to the December 14 conference
subfiles.about: Invites Phillips Petroleum to continue Green's discussion with Mr. Emery.
subfiles.summary: The Under Secretary asks Phillips Petroleum to send a representative to the December 14 meeting. The telegram explains that similar invitations were being sent to other interested companies.

subfiles.title: Frank A. Howard to Joseph C. Green after the industry meeting
subfiles.about: Reports that industry objections prevented unanimous agreement to withhold aviation-gasoline technology from Japan.
subfiles.summary: Howard says Standard Oil remained ready to cooperate but believed unilateral restraint would damage firms' earnings and competitive positions without an industry-wide agreement. He declines to advise other informed American interests about their duty and instead encloses a technical memorandum to assist further government deliberations.

subfiles.title: Memorandum on aviation gasoline
subfiles.to: Joseph C. Green and interested U.S. departments
subfiles.about: Explains the production, ownership, and military significance of high-octane aviation-gasoline technologies.
subfiles.summary: The memorandum describes octane requirements and sources of natural and synthetic aviation gasoline, including hydrogenation, catalytic cracking, hydroforming, tetraethyl lead, and several blending agents. It identifies the interlocking American and European companies controlling the relevant patents and technical knowledge and emphasizes that only the United States possessed complete information on all processes. The surviving portion ends while beginning an assessment of which techniques were already available to Japan.
